Annotation Tool: Which image is a better response to the user's request?
Image Wiki
Instructions
FAQ
Your task is to compare two generated images and choose the most interesting and beautiful one
Payment rules

To ensure fair compensation while maintaining high quality of the result, we employ the following procedure:

You will be required to work through 40 samples of training, which are very important to really understand the rules. The training is not paid for.
After that, you will have to take an exam, which is also not paid for. The exam consists of 30 tasks. If your accuracy exceeds 77%, you will be immediately passed to the real tasks. If your accuracy is lower, you will be shown 40 training tasks before the next exam of 30 tasks. This process repeats until accuracy of the last exam exceeds 77%.
The real tasks are paid $0.8 per hit. Each HIT consists of 20 tasks.
We will re-assess your performance from time to time. If it falls below certain thresholds, you will be asked to take the train and exam again.

The task is not difficult, but there are some rules and corner cases, so make sure to read the instruction carefully and approach training attentively.

Image Selection Annotation Guide
🎯 Task Goal

The main goal is to determine which of the two generated images is a better response to the user's request, which is described in the prompt and its accompanying images. The results of this annotation will help the model generate more accurate and relevant responses in the future.

🖥️ Interface Overview

The task interface consists of three main blocks:

1. The "Request" Block

This block contains the user's input.

Prompt: The instruction of what needs to be done.
Image Gallery: The source images for the prompt, which are required to generate a correct response. There can be a maximum of 10 images.
Detailed Analysis View: A field for closer inspection of an image (zoom, pan, etc.).
2. The "Response" Block

This block shows the AI model's generated output.

Image Gallery: The two images generated by the AI model in response to the "Request" block.
Selection Checkbox: Used to choose the better image as the answer. The keys 1 and 2 do the same thing without the mouse.
Detailed Analysis View: A field for closer inspection of an image.
3. The "Difference" Block

This block displays a heat map showing the difference between a selected source image and a selected generated image. It helps to more accurately identify what has changed in the generated image compared to the original.

Synchronized Control

You can zoom and pan the image in any of the three windows. All your actions—zooming in, zooming out, or moving the image—will be instantly and symmetrically mirrored in the other windows. - To Zoom: Use your mouse wheel. - To Pan/Move: Click and drag with your left mouse button.

Full-Size Viewer

For a closer look at a single image, open the full-size viewer. It shows one image at a time over the whole screen, which is the most reliable way to inspect small details, text, and fine artifacts.

To Open: Press the ⤢ Zoom button in the header of the "Request" or "Responses" block, or double-click the large image, or double-click a gallery thumbnail. The viewer opens on the image you clicked.
To Switch Images: Use the ← / → keys or the arrows on the sides. The viewer cycles only through the images of the block you opened: either the source images of the "Request" block, or the two generated images. So comparing Image 1 with Image 2 is a single keypress—the source images never get in the way.
To Switch Between Blocks: Press Tab or the ⇆ Request / ⇆ Responses button in the toolbar. This is how you compare a generated image with a source image without leaving the viewer. The zoom and position are preserved here as well. (If the task has no source images, this button is hidden.)
Image Counter: The pill in the top-left corner shows which image of the current block you are on (for example, Image 1 / 2 · Response — Image 1), so you always know what you are looking at after switching.
To Zoom: Use your mouse wheel (it zooms toward the mouse pointer), the + / - keys, or the toolbar buttons.
To Pan/Move: Click and drag with your left mouse button.
Zoom and Position Are Preserved: When you switch images with the arrows or jump to the other block, the current zoom level and position stay exactly the same. This lets you compare the same fragment of two images by flipping between them—a very convenient way to spot small differences. The view is reset only when you open the viewer or press Reset view (0).
Background: Press the background button in the toolbar (it shows the current color name) or B to cycle the backdrop behind the image: green → magenta → checkerboard → white → grey → black. The bright chroma-key colors help to see white, light, and semi-transparent areas, as well as the exact borders of the image.
To Close: Press Esc, the × button, or click the background next to the image.
Keyboard Shortcuts

Anywhere in the task:

1 / 2 — mark Image 1 / Image 2 as the better response (press again to unmark).
Enter — submit the answer and go to the next task.

Inside the full-size viewer:

← / → — previous / next image inside the current block.
Tab — jump between the request images and the responses.
+ / - or the mouse wheel — zoom in / out.
0 — reset zoom and position.
B — change the background.
Esc — close the viewer.

While the full-size viewer is open, 1, 2, and Enter are disabled, so an image cannot be selected and the task cannot be submitted by accident. Close the viewer first.

✅ Your Task

Using the checkboxes, you must select Image 1, Image 2, or both, depending on which image is a better response to the request in the first block. Instead of the checkboxes you can press 1 or 2, and then Enter to submit the answer and move on to the next task.

📋 Selection Criteria

The list below covers everything worth looking at. It is not a strict priority order — there is no rule that an earlier criterion automatically beats a later one. Read all of them, then judge each image as a whole and decide which one the person who sent the request would be happier to receive.

How to weigh the criteria
Prompt compliance is where you start, not where you stop. Check it first, but never decide on it alone. Whether both images follow the prompt well, both fail it, or one is closer than the other — in every one of these cases you still go through the remaining criteria before choosing a winner.
Weigh how bad each problem is, not which criterion it belongs to. A slightly wrong shade of blue and a hand with six fingers are both "failures", but they are not remotely equal. For every flaw you find, ask: how serious is it, how visible is it, and how much would it bother the person who asked for this image?
Trust what catches your eye first. Look at both images the way an ordinary viewer would — a few seconds, no zooming. Whatever problem you notice immediately is usually the one that decides the task. Use zoom afterwards to confirm what you already saw, not to hunt for flaws nobody would ever notice.
A perfect match to the prompt does not rescue a broken image. An image can follow the request to the letter and still be unusable: three legs, melted text, a face with two noses. If the other image misses a smaller part of the request but is otherwise clean, it is usually the better answer.
The reverse is equally true. A flawless image that ignores the request is not a good answer either. If one image misses the main point of what was asked, its sharpness and beauty do not save it.

Example. Image 1 does exactly what the prompt asked, but the character now has three legs. Image 2 made the background a slightly different shade of green than requested, and is otherwise clean. → Image 2 wins. A wrong shade is a small, forgivable miss; three legs ruins the image.

Example. Image 1 is sharp, beautiful and anatomically perfect, but the prompt asked to remove the car and the car is still there. Image 2 removed the car, with slightly visible edges around the gap. → Image 2 wins. It did the thing that was actually asked for.

Example. Both images follow the prompt well and neither has anatomy problems. → Keep going down the list: cohesion, artifacts, and finally overall quality and style match.

Prompt Compliance

The generated image must satisfy all requirements presented in the prompt.
If the prompt requires editing an original image (e.g., removing/adding/replacing elements), the generated image should ideally only change what was specified in the prompt. The rest of the image should remain unchanged (no quality improvements, no addition/removal of unmentioned elements). The heat map in the "Difference" block is designed for this analysis—the brighter the area, the greater the difference. If there's no difference, the heat map will be black.
Example:


Prompt compliance on its own does not decide the task. Whatever you find here — both images comply, both fail, or one is clearly closer — you must still go through the criteria below and weigh everything together (see How to weigh the criteria above).

Anatomical and Scene Correctness
Horses with six legs are not acceptable, unless explicitly asked for in the input prompt. Pay attention to details in prompts: sometimes horses with six legs are exactly what is needed. This criterion is not only about the anatomy of characters, but about the structure of all objects and their relationships, including printed text, cars, buildings, perspective, etc.
Example:

 

Image Cohesion
The generated image should not have elements that look artificially added or "pasted on." The image should appear as a single, cohesive whole.
Example:


Absence of Artifacts
Sometimes you will see objects being drawn on top of "circle blob" or "radial gradient" backgrounds, with watermarks or signatures, or surrounded by frames. They are not desired; please prefer images without them, unless the prompt explicitly asks for them.
Example:


Overall Image Quality
If the prompt is to generate a new image (not edit an existing one) and neither image has clear problems under the criteria above, you should evaluate the overall image quality (resolution, brightness, color saturation, etc.) and choose the higher-quality image.
Example:
 If the task involves editing or modifying existing images, prefer the generated image that better matches the overall style of the source images — including color palette, lighting, contrast, and visual style. The edited image should look like a natural continuation of the originals, not like a separately generated image.

⚠️ Important!
If it is impossible to determine a winner (both images perform equally across all selection criteria), you may mark both images. However, do this only in exceptional cases. Before making such a decision, please examine the images very carefully.

🎨 Special Case: Vector Images

Some prompts will involve tasks related to vector graphics. Therefore, it is important to know how to identify them.

Images of style "vector illustration" are expected to look like those drawn using vector graphics (see Wikipedia). Usually, they use only a few different colors at once, and shapes are filled with flat colors or simple color gradients. The presence of fine texture is a clear sign that it is not a vector. Shapes of objects can be arbitrarily complex.

Examples of Vector Images:
Vector illustrations use only flat colors or simple linear gradients and strictly no fine textures. The number of colors is also usually relatively small:





Note that shapes of objects may be very complicated and realistic. "Vector illustration" is vector mostly because of flat colors or simple gradients and the absence of textures.




This image is very detailed and complicated, but if you look closely, you will notice that there are only flat colors and simple gradients with clear, sharp transitions between segments of different colors—so this is a vector image.

Note that there are styles like engraving and lino-cut, which are vector images, despite looking quite complicated. The key is the same: a small number of colors (only 2 in the case of engraving and lino-cut), no gradients, and no textures.

FAQ
1. Overview of the Annotation Stages
Q: What stages should I expect when doing these tasks?
A: We use several stages to train, test, and ensure the quality of annotations:


Instruction Stage

You see detailed guidelines/markdown instructions. You must scroll through and click "Accept" to confirm you understand them before proceeding.



Training Stage

You receive a certain number of training tasks (samples).
If you submit an incorrect answer on a training task with ground truth, you’ll see a hint to guide you. You must re-try that same sample.
This stage helps you learn the interface and labeling expectations.



Exam Stage

After training, you move to an exam.
You must label a set of tasks without receiving hints for mistakes.
If you meet certain accuracy requirements (which we do not publicly disclose), you progress to Real Tasks; otherwise, you may return to Training.



Real Task Stage

Here you label the actual production tasks.
Occasionally, the system will insert “control” or “train-in-pool” tasks without telling you.
If your performance on these tasks falls short (criteria undisclosed), you may be returned to Training or, in rare cases, banned from further participation.



Ban Stage

If your accuracy stays below the required threshold after repeated attempts, the system may ban you from continuing.



2. How the Labeling Interface Works
Q: What does the interface look like and how do I use it?
A:

You typically see two images side by side.
Each image can be enlarged by clicking on it (a modal will appear with the full-size image). We strongly encourage you to enlarge images for detailed inspection.
You must choose a label (e.g., via radio buttons).
You can use keyboard hotkeys to speed up labeling:
1, 2, 3, 4 to select specific categories,
Enter to submit your current task.


Once you submit, you either get a new task or, if you reach 20 tasks in a HIT, you will be directed back to the MTurk submission page.

3. Task Expiration
Q: Do tasks expire if I wait too long?
A: Yes. Each assigned task has a time limit, shown in the labeling interface. If you fail to complete it before that limit expires, the task becomes invalid and you won’t get credit for it. If a task expires, you’ll need to request a new one.
4. Payment Rules on MTurk
Q: How do payments work for this project?
A:

You are paid per HIT on Amazon Mechanical Turk.
Each HIT consists of 20 tasks. Once you complete 20 tasks in that HIT, you will be redirected to MTurk’s submit page.
The exact payment rate for each HIT is shown on MTurk.
Our system typically reviews your submission within a few minutes and, once approved, you will see it credited to your MTurk account.

5. Contacting Us
Q: How can I contact the requester if I have questions or issues?
A: We handle communication exclusively via the MTurk platform. If you have concerns or run into technical issues, contact us through MTurk’s messaging system.
6. Review and Approval Time
Q: How long until my submission is approved?
A:

We aim to process your submission within a few minutes.
In rare cases (high load or manual checks), it can take longer, but typically it is automated and quick.
